meaning.en: A highly dangerous, threatening or hostile situation, especially one that somebody knowingly enters or becomes trapped in.

origin.statusEn: Exact Origin Unknown; Gradual Metaphorical Development
origin.statusZh: 確切來源不明；逐漸形成的比喻用法

history.en: Religious English has long used a lion’s mouth as an image of deadly danger and rescue, although this does not prove the origin of the modern idiom. Circus and sideshow performances later made the image literal. Early twentieth-century fiction describes performers placing their heads inside lions’ mouths. By 1949, a TIME article was already using put her head in the lion’s mouth figuratively to describe Eleanor Roosevelt taking a serious public risk.
history.zh: 宗教英語長久以來已使用「獅子之口」象徵致命危險及獲救，但這並不足以證明現代慣用語的確切來源。 其後，馬戲團及雜技表演把這個畫面變成真實動作。 二十世紀初的小說曾描寫表演者把頭放進獅子口中。 到了1949年，《時代》雜誌已用 put her head in the lion’s mouth 比喻 Eleanor Roosevelt 公開承受重大風險。

history.en: The physical act offered a natural metaphor: putting one’s head near a lion’s teeth means knowingly giving danger the chance to harm you. The exact first figurative use has not been firmly identified. Collins now records the full idiom as deliberately placing oneself in a dangerous or difficult situation.
history.zh: 這項真實動作自然形成了一個比喻：把頭放近獅子的牙齒，代表明知危險仍然讓自己暴露其中。 現時未能確定最早的比喻用法。 Collins 現在把完整表達解釋為故意令自己進入危險或困難處境。

origin.memoryEn: A head inside a lion’s mouth has almost no protection; a person in the lion’s mouth has entered a situation where serious harm may follow.
origin.memoryZh: 頭部一旦進入獅子口中，便幾乎沒有保護；身處 the lion’s mouth，便代表已進入可能帶來嚴重後果的處境。
